course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Cold War and Decolonization
unit.description: Study how the Cold War divided the world, how colonies won independence, how new states and movements challenged established power, and why the Cold War ended.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Harry S. Truman, president of the United States, inaugural address, January 20, 1949
stimulusBlocks.citation: Harry S. Truman, Inaugural Address, January 20, 1949. Text checked against the C-SPAN transcript in the NLTK corpus (inaugural/1949-Truman.txt).
stimulusBlocks.note: “That regime” is the government of the Soviet Union. Truman spoke two years after announcing aid to Greece and Turkey and while the Berlin airlift was still under way.
stimulusBlocks.text:
That regime adheres to a false philosophy which purports to offer freedom, security, and greater opportunity to mankind. Misled by this philosophy, many peoples have sacrificed their liberties only to learn to their sorrow that deceit and mockery, poverty and tyranny, are their reward.

That false philosophy is communism.

Communism is based on the belief that man is so weak and inadequate that he is unable to govern himself, and therefore requires the rule of strong masters.

Democracy is based on the conviction that man has the moral and intellectual capacity, as well as the inalienable right, to govern himself with reason and justice. . . .

Communism holds that the world is so deeply divided into opposing classes that war is inevitable.

Democracy holds that free nations can settle differences justly and maintain lasting peace.

questions.distinguisher: The superpowers occupied Germany together but divided it rather than cooperating.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 8.2 key concept: the United States and the Soviet Union competed for influence through alliances, aid, and military power
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the early Cold War in Europe, 1947–1955
stimulusBlocks.text:
In 1947, President Truman asked Congress for aid to Greece and Turkey to keep them from falling under communist control. This policy of containment aimed to stop the spread of Soviet influence. The Marshall Plan then sent about $13 billion to rebuild Western Europe's economies.

When the Soviet Union blockaded West Berlin in 1948, the United States and Britain supplied the city by air for almost a year. In 1949 the Western powers formed the NATO military alliance. The Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb that year, and in 1955 it organized the Warsaw Pact with its Eastern European satellites.

questions.distinguisher: The United States sent aid and advisers to Greece, not combat troops.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 8.2 key concept: some newly independent states sought to remain neutral in the Cold War through the Non-Aligned Movement
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the Bandung Conference and the Non-Aligned Movement, 1955–1961
stimulusBlocks.text:
In 1955, leaders of twenty-nine Asian and African countries met at Bandung, Indonesia. They condemned colonialism and called for economic cooperation among poorer nations. Many of the delegates had led independence struggles only a few years earlier.

In 1961, India's Jawaharlal Nehru, Egypt's Gamal Abdel Nasser, Indonesia's Sukarno, Ghana's Kwame Nkrumah, and Yugoslavia's Josip Broz Tito helped found the Non-Aligned Movement. Its members refused to join either Cold War bloc, though several accepted aid from both superpowers.

The scramble for Africa came in the 1880s.
questions.distinguisher: Bandung condemned colonialism, but it came during decolonization, not the scramble.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: John F. Kennedy, president of the United States, inaugural address, January 20, 1961
stimulusBlocks.citation: John F. Kennedy, Inaugural Address, January 20, 1961. Text checked against the C-SPAN transcript in the NLTK corpus (inaugural/1961-Kennedy.txt).
stimulusBlocks.note: “New States” are countries that had recently won independence from colonial rule; seventeen African colonies became independent in 1960 alone. “The deadly atom” refers to nuclear weapons.
stimulusBlocks.text:
Let every nation know, whether it wishes us well or ill, that we shall pay any price, bear any burden, meet any hardship, support any friend, oppose any foe, in order to assure the survival and the success of liberty. . . .

To those new States whom we welcome to the ranks of the free, we pledge our word that one form of colonial control shall not have passed away merely to be replaced by a far more iron tyranny. We shall not always expect to find them supporting our view. . . .

But neither can two great and powerful groups of nations take comfort from our present course -- both sides overburdened by the cost of modern weapons, both rightly alarmed by the steady spread of the deadly atom, yet both racing to alter that uncertain balance of terror that stays the hand of mankind's final war.

questions.prompt: Kennedy's audience for an inaugural address most likely led him to
choices: give a technical description of how nuclear weapons worked
propose detailed treaties with specific countries and leaders
criticize the American public for past mistakes in policy
state broad principles that reassure allies and warn rivals
questions.explanation: An inaugural address speaks to the nation and the world, so it states general commitments such as paying “any price.”
choiceExplanations: The address mentions the “deadly atom” but offers no technical detail.
The address states principles and not detailed treaties.
Inaugural addresses seek to unite listeners and do not blame them.
An inaugural address speaks to the nation and the world, so it states general commitments such as paying “any price.”
questions.distinguisher: Kennedy addressed arms control briefly, but a speech to a mass audience focuses on principles instead of terms of treaties.
